introTr: Bu hafta aktarma fiillerini, kısaltılmış cümlecikleri ve alışkanlık kalıplarını çalıştın. Bu deneme, bunları rahatça denemen için; yanlış yapmaktan korkma, her cevap öğretir.

items.q: The principal suggested ___ the meeting to Thursday.
She admitted ___ the files by mistake.

Please remember ___ the lights before you leave.
The students stopped ___ when the principal came in.
If the printer doesn't work, try ___ it off and on again.

items.q: The reports ___ before Friday.
She asked me ___ I had finished the report.
items.whyTr: Evet/hayır sorusunu aktarırken if / whether kullanılır.

passages.title: Getting used to Ohio
passages.text:
When Hafsa first moved to Ohio, nothing felt normal. In Isparta, she used to walk to the market every morning, buy fresh bread and talk with her neighbors for an hour. In Ohio, she had to drive to a big supermarket, and nobody wanted to talk. 'I'm not used to eating dinner at six,' she told Emre. 'At home, we ate at nine.'

The winter was the hardest part. Hafsa wasn't used to the snow, and she was afraid to drive. Her neighbor Linda, who has lived in Ohio all her life, taught her how to clean the car and drive slowly on ice. 'You'll get used to it,' Linda said.

Two years later, Hafsa still misses Isparta, but she has found new habits. She has started going to a Saturday farmers market, and she knows the names of five neighbors. Last week she even stopped to help a stranger push his car out of the snow.

questions.q: What did Hafsa use to do in Isparta?
options: She walked to the market and talked with neighbors.
questions.whyTr: Isparta'da her sabah pazara yürüyüp komşularla konuşurdu.

questions.q: Who helped Hafsa with winter driving?
questions.whyTr: Linda arabayı temizlemeyi ve buzda yavaş sürmeyi öğretti.

questions.q: What does the last paragraph suggest?
options: Hafsa has adapted to life in Ohio, but she still misses home.
questions.whyTr: Yeni alışkanlıklar edinmiş ama Isparta'yı özlüyor.

passages.title: Attendance policy
passages.text:
Attendance Policy - Oakridge Middle School

Students arriving after 8:00 a.m. must check in at the front office, where they will receive a late pass. Students arriving without a pass will not be admitted to class. Parents who know in advance that their child will miss school are asked to call the office before 9:00 a.m.

Absences are recorded as excused or unexcused. Absences caused by illness, medical appointments or family emergencies are excused when a note signed by a parent is submitted within three days. Students who miss more than ten days in a semester, excused or not, will be referred to the school counselor. The counselor may suggest a meeting with the family to discuss ways to improve attendance.

Teachers, including substitutes, are required to take attendance during the first ten minutes of class. Names of students arriving after the roll call must be sent to the office. Substitutes finding a mistake in the attendance list should report it to the front office immediately.

questions.q: What must a student arriving at 8:15 do?
options: Get a late pass at the front office
questions.whyTr: 8:00'den sonra gelenler ofisten geç kalma kağıdı alır.

options: When a signed parent note arrives within three days
questions.whyTr: Hastalık gibi sebeplerde, üç gün içinde imzalı not verilirse mazeretlidir.

questions.q: What happens after more than ten missed days in a semester?
options: The student is referred to the counselor.

questions.q: What should a substitute do if the attendance list has a mistake?
options: Report it to the front office

passages.title: Teachers from abroad
passages.text:
Every year, thousands of teachers from abroad come to work in American schools, attracted by higher salaries and new experiences. Most of them are surprised by how different the classroom culture is. In many countries, students stand when the teacher enters the room and rarely question what they are told. American students, on the other hand, are encouraged to speak up, to disagree politely and to work in groups.

'The hardest part was not the language,' said Maria, a math teacher from Spain, who joined a Texas school two years ago. 'It was learning that students call you by your last name, but they might also interrupt you with questions. At first I thought they were being rude. Now I understand they are showing interest.'

Schools that employ international teachers often provide mentors, helping newcomers understand local customs, discipline systems and paperwork. Administrators admit that the adjustment takes time. 'We advise new teachers not to expect perfection in the first semester,' one principal said. 'Within a year, most of them stop worrying and start enjoying the job.'

options: American students are encouraged to speak up.
questions.whyTr: Amerikan öğrenciler konuşmaya ve itiraza teşvik ediliyor.

questions.q: Why did Maria first think students were rude?
options: They called her by her first name.
questions.whyTr: Sözünü kesip soru soruyorlardı; sonra bunun ilgi olduğunu anladı.

questions.q: What does the principal advise new teachers?
questions.whyTr: 'We advise new teachers not to expect perfection.'

script.speaker: Mr. Reyes
script.text: Were you at the staff meeting yesterday, Hafsa?

script.speaker: Hafsa
script.text: I was. The principal announced that substitutes must now sign in electronically.

script.speaker: Mr. Reyes
script.text: I heard that too. She also warned everyone not to share passwords with students.

script.speaker: Hafsa
script.text: Yes. And Mrs. Lee suggested printing the sign-in sheets for people who don't have tablets.

script.speaker: Mr. Reyes
script.text: That's helpful. I've never been good with technology. I'm still not used to the new system.

script.speaker: Hafsa
script.text: Don't worry, you'll get used to it. I can show you after lunch.

questions.whyTr: Müdür substitute'lerin elektronik giriş yapması gerektiğini duyurdu.

questions.q: What did the principal warn about?
What does Hafsa offer to do?
options: Show Mr. Reyes the system after lunch
questions.whyTr: Hafsa öğle yemeğinden sonra sistemi göstermeyi teklif ediyor.

script.speaker: Mrs. Davis
script.text: Hello, this is Karen Davis, Ben's mother. His teacher said you had a problem with him yesterday?

script.speaker: Hafsa
script.text: Yes, Mrs. Davis. I'm the substitute. Ben was talking during the test, and I asked him to stop.

script.speaker: Hafsa
script.text: He denied talking, but two other students told me they heard him.

script.speaker: Mrs. Davis
script.text: He tends to talk when he is nervous. I'll speak to him tonight.

script.speaker: Hafsa
script.text: I appreciate that. I'd also suggest that he sit near the front. It might help him concentrate.

script.speaker: Mrs. Davis
script.text: That's a good idea. I'll mention it to his regular teacher.

questions.q: Why did Hafsa speak to Ben?
options: He was talking during the test.
Ben should take the test again.
Mrs. Davis should call the principal.
Ben should sit near the front.

script.speaker: Linda
script.text: Did you remember to mail the form, Hafsa?

script.speaker: Hafsa
script.text: Oh no, I forgot to mail it! I remember putting it in my bag this morning.

script.speaker: Hafsa
script.text: Here it is, on the back seat. Thank you!

script.speaker: Linda
script.text: The post office closes at five, so hurry.

writing.promptTr: Bir arkadaşına ABD'de hayata alışmayı anlatan e-posta yaz. Türkiye'de eskiden ne yapardın (used to), şimdi neye alıştın (be used to) ve neye henüz alışmaya çalışıyorsun (get used to)? Ayrıca bir toplantıda duyduğun bir tavsiyeyi aktar (suggested, advised, warned).
writing.promptEn: Write an email to a friend about getting used to life in the USA. Say what you used to do in Turkey, what you are used to now, and what you are still getting used to. Also report a piece of advice you heard (suggested, advised, warned).
checklistTr: 'Used to' ile eski bir alışkanlığı anlattım mı?
'Be used to / get used to' + -ing kullandım mı?
En az bir aktarma fiili kullandım mı (suggested ...ing, advised me to ...)?
Virgüllü bir ilgi cümleciği kullandım mı (Linda, who ...)?
writing.model:
Dear Ayse,

How are you? I have lived in Ohio for two years now, and I want to tell you how life has changed.

In Isparta, I used to walk to the market every morning and talk with my neighbors for an hour. Here, I have to drive everywhere, and people are usually in a hurry. I'm still not used to eating dinner at six, but I'm getting used to the quiet evenings. The winter was hard for me. I wasn't used to driving on snow, but my neighbor Linda, who has lived here all her life, taught me how to do it safely.

Last week at a school meeting, the principal advised substitute teachers to arrive thirty minutes early, and a teacher suggested making a seating chart on the first day. I think both ideas are very useful.

I miss Turkey, but I also love my new life. Please write to me soon!

Love,
Hafsa
